title: The manager who rewrites your order

beats.say: Why does Spark run faster when you describe what you want, instead of how to do it?

show.sub: Describe the result and Spark plans the work

beats.say: Picture a restaurant. You hand over an order slip. Before cooking, a manager reads it and tidies it up. Cross out dishes nobody wants. Check the small pantry, not the whole warehouse. That manager is Catalyst, Spark's planner.
Then the kitchen cooks. That is Tungsten. Ingredients sit in tight labelled boxes, and one cook finishes a whole recipe without passing plates around.
Now hand the manager a sealed envelope, a Python function. The manager cannot read it, so cannot improve it. And every item must be carried to another kitchen and back. Slow.

chip.text: Every row travels there and back

check.q: In the restaurant picture, what does Catalyst do?
opts: Reads and tidies the order before cooking
check.why: Catalyst is the planner. It rewrites the query before work starts. Tungsten is the kitchen that executes it.

work: Write down one Python function in your jobs and ask whether a built-in could replace it.
Ask your team who last read a query plan, and what they learned.

title: From one line to a compiled loop

beats.say: You write one line with a filter and a select. What happens in the milliseconds before Spark touches any data?

Catalyst first resolves names: does the column city exist, and what type is it? Then rules rewrite the logical plan. Filters move down toward the scan. Unused columns are dropped. A constant like sixty times twenty-four becomes one thousand four hundred forty once, not per row.
Next it generates several physical plans and picks one. For example, broadcast a small table to everyone, or shuffle both sides.

Tungsten then runs it. Rows sit in compact binary form outside Java objects, so there is less memory use and less garbage collection. A whole stage is compiled into one generated function, so a billion rows pass through one tight loop.

check.q: Why does pushing a filter toward the scan help?
opts: Fewer rows are read and carried through later steps
It converts the query to an RDD
check.why: Filtering early means less data is read and moved, which cuts work in every later step.

work: Run explain on a query and find where the filter sits relative to the scan.
Replace a repeated constant expression with a plain literal and check the plan folds it.

title: Reading a plan in order

beats.say: You run explain formatted and get forty lines. Where do you look first?

show.sub: Forty lines. Know what to scan for.

beats.say: Count the Exchange lines. Each one is a shuffle: data moving across the network. Exchange hashpartitioning city, 200 means rows are regrouped by city into 200 partitions. Shuffles are where most time and failures live.
Next, the FileScan. Look at PartitionFilters and PushedFilters. If both lists are empty, Spark is reading everything.

show.title: FileScan
items: PushedFilters: filters handed to the file reader
Both empty means a full scan

beats.say: Then the join. BroadcastHashJoin means a small table was sent to every executor, so the big side is not shuffled. SortMergeJoin means both sides were shuffled and sorted.
HashAggregate twice means a partial sum before the shuffle and a final one after. That is good: less data crosses the network.

check.q: A plan shows FileScan with empty PartitionFilters and empty PushedFilters, though your query has a where clause. What is likely?
opts: Spark is reading the whole dataset
check.why: Empty lists mean nothing was pruned or pushed, so the scan reads everything. The filter may be on a derived column or behind a UDF.

work: For your slowest job, count the Exchange operators and note which columns they partition by.
Check the FileScan in one big query for empty filter lists.

title: The black box and the changing plan

beats.say: Why can one innocent Python function make a job several times slower?

Catalyst treats a Python UDF as a black box. It cannot push a filter past it or prune columns around it. And Tungsten's compiled loop is broken: each row is serialised, sent to a Python process, computed, and sent back.
Fix one: use built-in functions, which Catalyst can see. Fix two: if you need Python, use a pandas UDF. It moves data in batches, so the transfer cost is paid once per batch, not once per row.

show.title: Cheaper options
items: Pandas UDF: data moves in batches

beats.say: One more gotcha. If the plan shows AdaptiveSparkPlan, it can change at run time. What explain shows before running may not be the final plan, for example a join switching to broadcast once real sizes are known.

chip.text: Real sizes can change the plan

check.q: Why is a pandas UDF cheaper than a plain Python UDF?
opts: It moves data to Python in batches
It avoids using Python at all
check.why: Batching spreads the transfer cost over many rows. Catalyst still cannot see inside it, and it still uses Python.

work: Search your code for udf and mark each one that a built-in function could replace.
When reading a plan with AdaptiveSparkPlan, also check the final plan in the Spark UI after the run.

title: Plans as a cost and review tool

beats.say: Your team's job cost doubled after a refactor. How do you find out why in five minutes?

Compare plans, not code. Run explain formatted before and after, and diff them. A new Exchange, an empty PushedFilters list, or a join flipping from broadcast to sort merge explains cost far faster than reading code.
Make it a habit. For critical pipelines, review the plan in code review, and treat the Exchange count as a budget. Each shuffle costs network, disk and a risk of failure.

show.title: Plan review
items: Review the plan for critical pipelines
Treat Exchange count as a budget
Each shuffle: network, disk, failure risk

beats.say: On UDFs, choose in order: built-in function, then pandas UDF, then plain Python UDF last. Use a plain one only when logic is truly irregular. Otherwise you pay serialisation on every row and blind the optimizer.

check.q: A refactor makes a job slower. Which finding in the plan best explains it?
opts: A new Exchange and empty PushedFilters
check.why: An extra shuffle and lost filter pushdown both mean more data read and moved. Adaptive execution and two aggregates are normal and often helpful.

work: Save explain output for your key jobs in version control and diff it on each change.
Set a team rule: any plain Python UDF needs a note on why no built-in or pandas option works.

title: Counting ballots: how Spark splits work

beats.say: How would a hundred helpers count a million ballots by city, when the ballots sit in a hundred separate boxes?

First, each helper works alone on one box. They toss invalid ballots and tally their own box by city. Nobody talks to anyone. Spark calls that a narrow step, and it chains many of them together for free.

Now the hard part. Every Chicago tally must land on one table. So each helper sorts tallies into piles by city and hands them over. That handover is a shuffle. It is slow, because everyone talks to everyone.
Table workers add up their piles and announce totals. If a helper vanishes, Spark simply redoes that box from the written instructions, so nothing needs copying.

check.q: Why is the step where helpers hand tallies to city tables the slow one?
opts: Each helper has to read the ballots twice
Every helper sends data to many tables over the network
The tables can only count one ballot at a time
check.why: A shuffle moves data between many machines so rows for the same city meet. Work done inside one box needs no such movement.

work: Next time you read a query, mark each step as narrow (no movement) or wide (movement).
Count how many wide steps your slowest job has.

title: One query, two stages, 280 tasks

beats.say: You wrote three lines of code. So how many tasks did Spark actually run?

Filter is narrow: each output partition comes from one input partition, so it runs inside a stage. Group by is wide: it needs rows from many partitions, so it forces a shuffle and ends the stage. Only show, the action, starts a job.

Say the table is ten gigabytes, read in one hundred twenty eight megabyte splits. That is about eighty tasks in stage one. Each filters its slice, counts per city, and writes partial counts to shuffle files, grouped by hash of city.

Stage two defaults to two hundred tasks. Each reads its share of those files, sees every row for its cities, and finishes the count. Eighty plus two hundred: two hundred eighty tasks, from one tiny query.

check.q: In the query, what ends stage one and starts stage two?
opts: The filter, because it removes rows
The show call, because it is an action
The group by, because it needs rows from many partitions
check.why: A wide transformation needs a shuffle, and the shuffle is the stage boundary. Filter is narrow, and show starts the job but does not itself cut a stage.

work: Open a slow job in the Spark UI and match each stage to the wide step that created it.
Check how many tasks each stage ran and compare it to your input size divided by split size.

title: Lazy plans, skew and lost shuffle files

beats.say: You call count, then show, on the same dataframe. Does Spark read the files once?
No, twice. Transformations are lazy, and every action starts a fresh job that replays the plan from the files. If you reuse a result, cache it, or you pay for the whole read again.

A group by count shuffles little, because stage one counts inside each partition first. Partial counts cross the network, not raw rows. But skew still bites. If one city holds half the rows, one task does half the work, and the whole stage waits for it.
When an executor dies, Spark recomputes its lost partitions from lineage. But shuffle files live on that machine's disk, so without an external shuffle service, the earlier stage reruns too.

check.q: A group by count has one city with half of all rows. What happens?
opts: Stage one slows down because it must send raw rows
One stage two task is much slower and the stage waits for it
Spark automatically splits the city in every case
check.why: Rows for one key go to one task after the shuffle, so a hot key makes a straggler. Stage one pre-counts, so it is not the problem, and splitting needs adaptive execution or salting.

work: Cache any dataframe that more than one action uses, and unpersist it when done.
In the Spark UI, compare max task time to median task time in each stage to spot skew.

title: Fix slow Spark jobs in the right order

beats.say: A job runs for two hours. Do you add executors? Usually, no.

Fix it in order. One, read less: filter early and select only the columns you need. Two, avoid the shuffle: broadcast a small table so the join needs none. Three, shape the shuffle: aim for about one hundred to two hundred megabytes per partition, and let adaptive execution merge small ones and split skewed ones. Four, add hardware.

show.title: Fix in this order
items: 1. Read less: filter and prune columns
2. Avoid the shuffle: broadcast small tables
3. Shape it: 100 to 200 MB partitions, adaptive execution

beats.say: Why this order? Every shuffle writes to disk and crosses the network, which costs far more than computing. Extra executors just give more workers a longer wait on the same skewed task.
Lineage recovery is cheap for short pipelines. In a long iterative job, a failure replays everything. There, checkpoint: pay for a disk write to get a short recovery.

check.q: A two-hour job has one task running far longer than the rest. What should you try before adding executors?
opts: Double the executor count so the slow task gets more help
Fix the skew, for example with adaptive skew handling or salting the key
Cache every dataframe in the job
check.why: A single task cannot be shared across executors, so extra hardware does not shorten it. Splitting the hot key does.

work: Write a tuning checklist in order: read less, avoid shuffle, shape partitions, then hardware.
Turn on adaptive execution and compare shuffle partition sizes before and after.
Add a checkpoint to any iterative job with more than a few dozen steps.

title: Joins as photocopies and sorting

beats.say: How do you match a huge pile of orders with a tiny list of customer names, without moving the huge pile?

Picture fifty workers, each holding a stack of delivery slips. You also have a one page list of zone names. Photocopy that page and hand a copy to every worker. Now each worker looks up names at their own desk. Nobody carries the heavy stacks anywhere.

That is a broadcast join. The copy is cheap because the list is small. If both piles are huge, copying will not work. Then everyone must sort both piles by zone and send matching slips to the same table. Slower, but it works at any size. Spark picks for you.

show.title: Two ways to match
items: Small side: copy it to everyone
Both huge: sort and regroup by key

check.q: In the analogy, why is photocopying the list to every worker a good idea?
opts: Because the list is small, so copying is cheap and the big stacks never move
Because it sorts the stacks faster
check.why: Broadcast works when one side is small enough to copy everywhere, which avoids moving the large side.

work: List the joins in one of your jobs and mark which side is small.
Check whether those small tables are really tiny, in megabytes.

title: Four ways Spark joins

beats.say: A two terabyte trips table meets a five megabyte zones table. Why would you shuffle two terabytes for that?

You would not. Spark sees zones is under ten megabytes, the default broadcast threshold. The driver collects it and sends a copy to every executor. Each executor builds a hash map, then scans its own trips partitions and looks up zone ids. No trips row ever crosses the network.

chip.text: No shuffle of the big side

beats.say: Now make both tables huge. Spark uses sort merge join. It hashes the join key to send matching keys to the same partition, two hundred by default. Each side is sorted there, then merged in one pass. The cost is the shuffle, which writes to disk and moves data over the network.
No equality condition means nested loops: every row against every row.

show.sub: Nested loop: avoid on large data

check.q: A 3 TB table joins a 4 MB table on an equality key. What does Spark do by default?
opts: Broadcast hash join, with no shuffle of the big table
check.why: 4 MB is under the 10 MB default threshold, so the small side is broadcast and the big table stays put.

work: Open the Spark UI SQL tab and read the join type on your slowest query.
Look for Exchange nodes: each one is a shuffle you are paying for.

title: Where joins go wrong

beats.say: Why does broadcasting a table that is only eight hundred megabytes crash the driver?

Because the driver must first collect the whole table, then send it out. On disk it is compressed. In memory, as a hash map, it can be several times bigger. And it needs that room on the driver and on every executor at once. Wrong size estimates from stale statistics make this worse.

chip.text: Memory use is far above file size

beats.say: Sort merge has its own trap: skew. If one key holds half the rows, one partition gets half the data, and one task runs for an hour while the rest finish in seconds. Adaptive query execution can help. It reads real shuffle sizes, may switch to broadcast, and splits skewed partitions.

check.q: One task in a sort-merge join runs far longer than the others. Most likely cause?
opts: The broadcast threshold is too low
A hot join key sent too many rows to one partition
The driver is collecting the table
check.why: Skewed keys land in one shuffle partition, so a single task does most of the work.

work: Compare max and median task duration in the Spark UI stage page to spot skew.
Enable adaptive query execution and its skew join setting, then re-measure.
Refresh table statistics so size estimates are trustworthy.

title: Choosing a join strategy at scale

beats.say: When is the fastest join the one you should refuse to use?

Broadcast avoids the shuffle, but every executor holds its own copy. A five hundred megabyte table on two hundred executors means one hundred gigabytes of memory, plus driver risk. A table that grows each month turns a fast job into a midnight outage. So hint only for small, stable dimensions, and leave the threshold modest.

For two big tables, shrink the shuffle instead. Filter and select columns before joining. Write both tables bucketed on the join key, so later joins skip the shuffle. Salt hot keys. Try shuffled hash only when one side is much smaller and partitions fit in memory, since it skips the sort but risks running out of memory.

show.title: Big-to-big playbook
items: Bucket both tables on the join key
Shuffled hash only if one side is much smaller

check.q: A dimension table grows 20 percent monthly and is currently broadcast with a hint. Best move?
opts: Remove the hard hint, let adaptive execution choose, and monitor size
check.why: A growing table will eventually break a forced broadcast. Letting the engine choose from real sizes is safer.

work: Add a size alert on tables you force-broadcast.
Bucket your largest repeated join pair on the shared key.
Document why each broadcast hint exists and when to revisit it.

title: One checkout lane, everyone queuing

beats.say: Why does a job with a hundred workers sometimes run as if it had only one?

Picture a supermarket with a hundred checkout lanes. Each shopper is sent to a lane by their home city. If eighty of every hundred shoppers come from Bengaluru, they all join one queue. The other lanes sit empty.
That is skew. A few popular keys, meaning the labels we group by, hold most of the rows. The whole job waits for the slowest lane, so one task can take an hour while the rest finish in seconds.

show.title: Skew
items: A few keys hold most rows
One task does most of the work
The job waits for the slowest

beats.say: The cure is to open more lanes for the busy city, and split its shoppers between several cashiers.

check.q: Why does skew make a whole Spark job slow?
opts: Too many workers fight over memory
The job finishes only when its slowest task finishes
Hot keys are stored on slower disks
check.why: Work is grouped by key, so one overloaded task holds up the stage while the others sit idle.

work: Name the one or two keys in your biggest table that hold the most rows.
Ask what share of rows the top key has before you design a join or group by.

title: Why one task runs for an hour

beats.say: Why does one Spark task run for almost an hour when the median task takes seconds?

After a shuffle, Spark hashes each key and sends every row with that key to one partition. At Meridian, Bengaluru has eighty percent of trips. So a join or group by city sends eighty percent of the data to a single task.
In the Spark UI stage page, the signature is clear. The median task takes seconds, the maximum takes most of an hour. Shuffle read size shows the same lopsided pattern.

Adaptive execution handles much of this. A partition counts as skewed if it is over five times the median and over 256 megabytes. Spark splits it into several tasks and copies the matching rows from the other side.

show.title: Adaptive skew split
items: Spot partition over 5x median and 256 MB
Copy matching rows from other side

check.q: When does adaptive execution treat a partition as skewed?
opts: Larger than five times the median and larger than 256 MB
Any partition holding a NULL key
Any partition bigger than the median
check.why: Both conditions must hold: more than five times the median size and more than 256 MB.

work: Open the stage page of a slow job and compare median and max task time.
Check shuffle read size per task to confirm the skew before you change code.

title: Why adaptive handling is not enough

beats.say: Adaptive skew handling is on, yet your job is still slow. What did it miss?
It splits skewed partitions in sort-merge joins, and copies the other side's matching rows. It does not rescue every shape of query. Check the stage page again to see whether a straggler remains.

show.title: Limits of adaptive
items: Needs partition over 5x median and 256 MB

beats.say: NULL keys are a trap. Every NULL hashes to the same partition, so they pile up in one task. If NULL or junk keys can never match, filter them out before the join.
Salting adds a random number from zero to fifteen to the big side's key, and repeats each small-side row sixteen times. For an aggregation, do two steps: by key and salt, then by key alone.

show.title: Salting
show.text:
salt = int(rand() * 16)
explode small side over 0..15
join on city and salt

check.q: Why must an aggregation use two steps after salting?
opts: The first step spreads the hot key, the second combines the pieces back per key
The second step removes NULL keys
check.why: Partial results exist per key and salt, so a second aggregation by key alone merges them into one answer.

work: Count NULL keys in each join column and filter those that cannot match.
Test salting on a copy with a small salt count and compare the max task time.

title: Choosing a skew fix, cheapest first

beats.say: Salting always works, so why is it the last fix you should reach for?
Salting makes the small side sixteen times bigger, adds code to maintain, and an aggregation needs two stages. A higher salt count spreads the hot key more but multiplies that copy cost.
So go in order. First check adaptive handling is on, since it is free. Second, broadcast the small side, which removes the shuffle entirely. Third, filter NULL and junk keys.
Fourth, handle a known hot key alone. Broadcast join its one matching row, join the rest normally, and union. Salt only when hot keys are many or unknown.

show.title: Hot keys
items: 4. Split out hot key, broadcast join
Join the rest normally, then union

check.q: Bengaluru is the single known hot key and the city table is tiny. Which fix fits best?
check.why: A tiny dimension table can be broadcast, so there is no shuffle and no skewed partition, at far lower cost than salting.

work: Write the fix order as a checklist in your team's Spark runbook.
Before salting, measure the cost of copying the small side by the salt count.
Record which keys are hot so you can choose between a hot-key split and salting.

title: Sizing a job: the moving day

beats.say: How many movers do you hire to empty a warehouse by tonight? Too few and you miss the deadline. Too many and they trip over each other.

show.sub: Too few is slow. Too many is wasteful.

beats.say: Think of your data as boxes. Spark packs them into batches called partitions, so each worker carries one batch at a time. Pick a sensible batch size, and the number of batches follows.
The workers are the cores. Group them into trucks, called executors. Each truck needs enough space for the batch it carries, plus room to sort things inside.

chip.text: Truck space must fit the batch

beats.say: So sizing is simple. Count the boxes, time one trip, then choose trucks and workers to finish on time. Rent extra trucks only while boxes are waiting.

show.title: The whole method
items: Pick trucks and workers for your deadline
Rent extra only while work waits

check.q: In the moving analogy, what does an executor correspond to?
opts: A truck holding several workers and their space
check.why: An executor is a process with a few cores (workers) and its own memory (space). Partitions are the batches of boxes it carries.

work: Write down your biggest job's input size and how many partitions its widest stage has.
Ask what deadline the job really needs before you ask for more machines.

title: Sizing a one terabyte job

beats.say: You have one terabyte to process. How do you choose a cluster size without guessing?

show.sub: Work it out in four steps

beats.say: Start with partitions. One terabyte at about 128 megabytes each is roughly 8,000 partitions in the widest stage. Each partition becomes one task.
Next, cores. Time one task. If it takes one minute and you want to finish in about ten minutes, eight thousand tasks must run in ten waves. That needs around 800 cores.

Pack four or five cores per executor, so about 160 to 200 executors. More and threads fight over disk and garbage collection. If a task needs four times its partition, that is 512 megabytes, so five tasks need about 2.5 gigabytes plus headroom.

show.title: Per executor
items: Task memory: several times partition size
5 tasks at 512 MB is 2.5 GB, add headroom

check.q: A stage has 8,000 tasks of one minute each, and you want it done in about ten minutes. Roughly how many cores do you need?
check.why: Ten waves of tasks means 8,000 divided by 10, which is 800 tasks running at once, so about 800 cores.

work: Time a single task on a sample partition before you request cores.
Set executor cores to four or five, then size memory from partition size times a safety factor.

title: Dynamic allocation and its traps

beats.say: You turn on dynamic allocation, and the job fails with missing shuffle files. Why would releasing an idle executor break anything?
Executors do not only compute. They also hold shuffle output, the files later stages read. Remove an idle executor, and those files vanish, so downstream tasks must recompute or fail.
The fix is keeping shuffle data alive without the executor. Use an external shuffle service, or shuffle tracking, which refuses to remove executors that still hold needed shuffle data.

show.title: Two safe ways
items: External shuffle service serves files after removal
Shuffle tracking keeps executors that hold live data

beats.say: Other traps. Over five cores per executor causes disk and garbage collection contention. Too little memory per task spills to disk or runs out during joins and sorts. Set a maximum executor count to protect the cluster.

show.title: Gotchas
items: Over 5 cores: I/O and GC contention
Low memory: spills or out of memory

check.q: Why does dynamic allocation need an external shuffle service or shuffle tracking?
opts: Because removed executors would take their shuffle files with them
check.why: Executors store shuffle output that later stages read. Without a service or tracking, scaling down deletes that data and forces recompute or failure.

work: Check that your dynamic allocation setup has shuffle tracking or an external shuffle service enabled.
Set a max executors limit so one job cannot take the whole cluster.

title: Sizing as an architect

beats.say: Sizing math gives a starting point, not an answer. So where does it break, and what do you decide around it?
Production jobs use cluster mode, so the driver runs inside the cluster. In client mode, the driver lives on a laptop or edge node, and if that dies, the job dies with it.
On YARN, executors are containers on a shared Hadoop cluster. On Kubernetes, they are pods, so you also weigh pod startup time and rely on shuffle tracking for scale down.

show.title: Where it runs
items: Kubernetes: driver and executors are pods
Dynamic allocation: good for bursty jobs
Fixed size: good for steady, tight deadlines

beats.say: Skew breaks the math. One huge partition holds up the stage, however many cores you add. Fix skew first, then right-size from measured task times, because idle cores are cost.

show.title: Stage time with one skewed task

check.q: A stage waits on one task that is 25 times slower than the rest. What is the best first move?
opts: Fix the skew in the data
Raise cores per executor to ten
check.why: The slow task sets the stage time. Extra cores sit idle, so you remove the skew, then size using measured task times.

work: Run production jobs in cluster mode so they do not depend on one machine.
Look at the slowest task versus the median in each stage before adding hardware.
Choose dynamic allocation for bursty workloads and fixed size for steady, deadline-bound ones.

title: A satnav for your query

beats.say: Would you plan a road trip once, then ignore every traffic jam?

show.sub: That is how old Spark worked

beats.say: Old Spark did exactly that. Before the job ran, it drew a route using guesses about how much data each step would produce. Those guesses were often wrong.
Adaptive query execution works like a satnav. After each leg of the trip, it looks at the real traffic and picks the route again.

It does three things. It merges lots of tiny piles of work into sensible ones. It swaps in a faster way to combine two tables when one turns out small. And it splits one giant pile so a single worker is not stuck.

show.title: Three fixes
items: Swap to a faster join when a table is small

check.q: What is the main idea behind adaptive query execution?
opts: Re-plan between stages using real data sizes
Plan the job more carefully before it starts
check.why: It waits until a stage finishes, measures the actual output, and then chooses the rest of the plan, instead of trusting early estimates.

work: Check whether your cluster has adaptive execution switched on, and what Spark version it runs.
Find one slow job whose plan relied on a size estimate and compare it to the real size.

title: What AQE changes at run time

beats.say: Why did your Spark job once run two hundred tiny tasks for ten megabytes of data?
Because the plan was fixed up front. Spark defaults to two hundred shuffle partitions, which are the chunks of data sent between stages, whatever the real size.

Now Spark finishes a stage, then reads the actual size of each shuffle output. Tiny neighbouring partitions are merged toward a target near sixty-four megabytes. Two hundred small tasks become maybe three.

It also rechecks joins. Say a sort-merge join was planned, but a filter shrank one side to eight megabytes. That is under the ten megabyte broadcast limit, so Spark sends that table to every worker instead. Sorting the big side is skipped.

check.q: A planned sort-merge join has one side that shrinks to 8 MB after a filter. What can AQE do?
opts: Turn it into a broadcast join
check.why: Once the real size is known to be under the broadcast threshold, AQE swaps the strategy and avoids sorting the large side.

work: Set the initial shuffle partition count high and let coalescing shrink it, rather than hand-tuning per job.
Open the Spark UI for a finished job and compare partition counts before and after coalescing.

title: Where AQE stops helping

beats.say: If AQE is on, why is one task still running for an hour?
AQE only re-plans at shuffle boundaries, once a stage has finished and its output sizes are known. It cannot fix a skewed task that is already running.

Its skew fix works for joins. If one partition is much bigger than the median, by default five times and above two hundred fifty-six megabytes, Spark splits it into pieces and joins each against a copy of the other side. A skewed group by is not helped.
A plan with no shuffle has nothing to adapt. And skew in a window function still needs salting by hand.

show.title: Still on you
items: Group by skew is not split

check.q: Which job is least likely to be rescued by AQE's skew handling?
opts: A sort-merge join with one hot key
A group by with one hot key
A join where one partition is 10 times the median
check.why: AQE splits skewed partitions in joins. A skewed aggregation or window still sends the hot key to one task, so you need salting or pre-aggregation.

work: Find your slowest long-tail tasks in the Spark UI and note whether they come from a join or an aggregation.
Keep a salting recipe ready for group by and window skew.

title: Spark 2 to 3: what really breaks

beats.say: Adaptive execution gets the headline, but where do Spark 2 to 3 migrations actually break?

Not in the speed features. Dynamic partition pruning is a bonus. Filter a small dimension table, and Spark skips fact table partitions at run time, so a question about one store reads one slice, not the whole year.

chip.text: Skips partitions it does not need

beats.say: The breakage is stricter behaviour. Spark 3 changed date and timestamp parsing, so a pattern that quietly worked before may now throw an error or return different values. ANSI mode, strict about bad casts and overflow, raises errors instead of returning null.

show.title: Where it breaks
items: ANSI mode errors on bad casts

beats.say: Rerun old jobs side by side and diff the outputs before you cut over.

check.q: What is the most common source of migration breakage from Spark 2 to 3?
opts: Adaptive execution picking a worse plan
Stricter SQL and date parsing behaviour
check.why: The performance features rarely change results, but stricter parsing and ANSI-style behaviour can change values or raise errors in old queries.

work: Run old and new Spark versions side by side on real data and diff the results.
Grep your code for date format patterns and casts that relied on lenient parsing.

title: Trusting AQE as an architect

beats.say: Should you just turn on AQE and stop tuning?

show.text: Turn it on and stop tuning?

beats.say: Mostly yes. It is on by default since Spark 3.2, costs little, and fixes the worst guesses. Set the initial partition count high, and let it merge down.

But it is not free. It adds stage barriers, since the plan waits for real sizes, and it cannot reorder joins or fix a bad data model. A big table joined on a hot key still deserves salting or a pre-aggregation.

show.title: Limits
items: Stage barriers while it waits for sizes
Cannot fix a bad data model
Hot keys still need salting or pre-aggregation

beats.say: For a staff answer: lean on AQE for variance across days, hint joins when you know the sizes, and watch the Spark UI for the final plan to confirm it actually changed anything.

show.title: Your playbook
items: Check the final plan in the UI

check.q: Your daily job has a hot customer key that dominates a group by. What is the best answer?
opts: Rely on AQE skew handling alone
Pre-aggregate or salt the key, and keep AQE on
Disable AQE and raise partitions to 2000
check.why: AQE splits skew in joins, not aggregations. Salting or pre-aggregation fixes the hot key, and AQE still helps with partition sizing and join strategy.

work: Write down when you would hint a join despite AQE, such as known small dimension tables.
Add a check that reads the final adaptive plan for your slowest job after each release.

title: Let the calculator count

beats.say: Would you ask a brilliant friend to add up ten thousand receipts by hand?
Probably not. They would lose count somewhere. A calculator never does. So let the calculator add, and let your friend decide what the totals mean.
An AI agent reading a Spark job log is that friend. The log is millions of lines of tiny records, about how long each piece of work took. Code adds them up into a short table of five rows.
Now the agent sees one worker took ten minutes while the others took ten seconds. That is a clear clue, and reading clues is what it is good at.

check.q: Why give the agent a five-row summary instead of the raw log?
opts: Models are poor at counting over thousands of lines but good at interpreting a short summary
Raw logs are not allowed by Spark
Summaries make the Spark job run faster
check.why: Code is reliable at arithmetic. The model adds value by interpreting a small, shaped table.

work: Find one place where you paste raw logs into a model and ask what could be counted by code first.
Write down the three numbers you would want summarized from a slow job.

title: From fifty megabytes to five rows

beats.say: How do you turn a fifty megabyte Spark log into twelve numbers?
The code reads the log one line at a time. It keeps only task end events. Each one holds a launch time, a finish time, bytes of shuffle read, and bytes spilled to disk. It groups them by stage.

For each stage it computes the median task time, the maximum task time, the biggest shuffle read, and total spill. Median is the middle value. If the median is four seconds and the maximum is ninety, one task is dragging the whole stage. That is skew.
It sorts by maximum task time and returns the top five. The model gets five small rows, not a million lines.

check.q: A stage has median task time 4 seconds and maximum 90 seconds. What does this most suggest?
opts: Skew: one task has far more work than the rest
The cluster has too many executors
check.why: Healthy stages have tasks of similar length. A maximum far above the median is the skew signature.

work: Run the summary on one of your own event logs and compare median to max for each stage.
Flag any stage where max is more than ten times the median.

title: When the summary lies

beats.say: Your summary tool says no skew. Could it still be wrong?

Yes. Event log field names change between Spark versions. This code uses get with a default of zero, so a renamed field silently becomes zero. The tool then reports no spill when there was plenty. Check names against one of your own logs.

Other gaps. Failed or retried tasks also appear as task end events, so they inflate counts. Metrics can be missing for killed tasks. And the maximum shows one slow task, not why. It could be skew, a bad node, or garbage collection.

show.title: Other gotchas
items: Causes: skew, bad node, garbage collection

beats.say: So treat the output as a hypothesis. Check it against the Spark UI before you act.

show.sub: The Spark UI is the evidence

check.q: Why is using get with a default of zero risky in this tool?
opts: It makes the log read slower
A renamed field silently reads as zero and hides real spill or shuffle
It deletes failed tasks from the log
check.why: Missing keys do not raise errors, so a version change can produce confident but wrong zeros.

work: Check each field name in your parser against a real log from your Spark version.
Make the tool report how many tasks had missing metrics.

title: Tools over big context

beats.say: Why not just give the model the whole log and a big context window?

Cost and reliability. Fifty megabytes is millions of tokens, paid on every call, and models miscount over thousands of lines. A tool that returns five rows costs almost nothing and gives the same answer every time.

The trade-off is that you decide in advance what to count. If skew hides in a column you did not summarize, the agent is blind. So add a second tool, explain formatted, to link a slow stage to its operator. Keep tools few, with descriptions saying when to use them.
Last, process. Diagnose the job yourself first and write it down. Then run the agent. Its answer is a hypothesis, and the Spark UI is the evidence. Skip that and you anchor on its answer.

check.q: What is the main limit of a precomputed summary tool?
opts: It costs more than sending the raw log
You must decide in advance what to count, so unsummarized signals are invisible
It cannot be used with more than one Spark version
check.why: Shaped output is cheap and reliable but only shows what you chose to compute, so add tools or check the UI for the rest.

work: Write your own diagnosis of a slow job before running the agent, then compare.
Write each tool description to say when to use it.
List signals your summary misses, such as skew in a key column.

title: The cook, the counter and the pantry

beats.say: What happens when the pot you are cooking in is bigger than your kitchen counter?

show.sub: That is Spark running short of memory

beats.say: Think of an executor as a cook. The counter is execution memory, where the work happens: sorting, joining, adding up. When the counter fills, the cook moves some food to the pantry shelf, which is disk. Work continues, but every trip to the pantry is slow.

show.title: When the counter *fills*, food goes to the pantry

chip.text: Spill: slow but it keeps going

beats.say: That slow trip is called a spill. It is an early warning, not a failure. But if one single ingredient is too big to ever move, like a whole cow, the cook gives up. That is an out of memory error.

chip.text: Spill is a warning, OOM is the crash

check.q: In the kitchen analogy, what does a spill correspond to?
opts: The cook quitting because the pot is too big
Moving food from the counter to the slow pantry so work can continue
check.why: A spill moves data from fast memory to disk. The job slows down but carries on. Quitting is the out of memory error.

work: Open the Spark UI stage page and check the spill columns for your slowest job.
Treat any non-zero spill as an early warning and note which stage it appears in.

title: Where an executor's memory goes

beats.say: Why does a ten gigabyte executor not give you ten gigabytes to work with?

show.text: 10 GB executor ≠ 10 GB to work with

beats.say: Say the heap is ten gigabytes. About sixty percent, six gigabytes, is unified memory. Execution and storage share it and borrow from each other. Execution handles shuffles, joins and sorts. Storage holds cached data. The rest is user memory, for your own objects.

Outside the heap sits overhead: at least three hundred eighty four megabytes, or ten percent. Here that is one gigabyte. It holds off-heap buffers and Python worker processes. The container is about eleven gigabytes in total, and if it goes over, the cluster manager kills it.

nodes.label: Container limit 11 GB
nodes.sub: go over and it is killed

beats.say: When execution runs short, Spark spills to disk and keeps going, slowly. Watch the spill columns in the UI.

show.title: Out of room in execution
items: Spark spills to disk and continues
Spill columns in the UI are the early warning

check.q: An executor has a 10 GB heap and default overhead of 10 percent. What is the approximate container size the cluster manager enforces?
check.why: The container is heap plus overhead: 10 GB plus about 1 GB. Going over that limit gets the container killed, even if the heap is fine.

work: Write down heap, unified memory and overhead for your biggest job's executors.
When sizing a cluster, request container size, not just heap size.

title: cache, persist and checkpoint

beats.say: You cached a DataFrame and the job got slower. How is that possible?

Cache stores a DataFrame after its first computation, in memory, spilling to disk if needed. Persist is the same, but you choose the storage level. Later actions read the stored copy instead of recomputing.

chip.text: persist = cache plus your storage level

beats.say: But cached data lives in the same unified memory that joins and sorts need. Cache something used once, and you only crowd out execution and cause spills. So cache only what several actions reuse and is costly to rebuild. Then call unpersist.

show.title: Cache with care
items: Cache shares memory with joins and sorts
Use it only if reused by more than one action

beats.say: Checkpoint is different. It writes data to reliable storage and throws away the lineage, the recipe of steps. Use it to cut a very long plan, as in iterative jobs, and for streaming state.

check.q: A DataFrame is used by exactly one action. What does cache do for it?
opts: Nothing useful, and it takes memory that execution could use
check.why: Cache only pays off on reuse. For a single use it costs memory shared with joins and sorts, which can cause more spill.

work: Audit every cache call: does more than one action reuse it, and is it costly to rebuild?
Add unpersist after the last use of each cached DataFrame.

title: Matching the error to the cause

beats.say: Three different memory errors, three different fixes. Do you know which is which?

show.sub: Read the error before touching a setting

beats.say: A java out of memory error on an executor means one partition was too big. Think skew, too few partitions, or a join that explodes rows. A hash map for one hot key cannot spill, so the executor dies. Fix the data shape: more partitions, handle skew, filter earlier.

Container killed for exceeding memory limits is different. The heap was fine. Overhead ran out, often from Python UDFs or big off-heap buffers. Raise memory overhead, and swap row by row UDFs for built-in functions.

check.q: Containers keep being killed for exceeding memory limits, but heap usage looks low. Which first response fits best?
opts: Raise memoryOverhead and replace row UDFs with built-ins
check.why: The heap is fine, so overhead is exhausted, often by Python workers or off-heap buffers. That points to overhead and built-in functions.

work: When a job fails, record the exact error text before changing any setting.
Replace the heaviest Python row UDFs with built-in functions.

title: Driver crashes and the daily slowdown

beats.say: The driver crashes, and nobody touched the executors. Why?

show.sub: The coordinator ran out of room

beats.say: The driver coordinates the job. Collect pulls the entire result into its memory, so collect on a large result kills it. A broadcast that is too big is built on the driver first, with the same result. Remove the collect, write results out, and lower the broadcast threshold.

Then there is the job that gets slower every day, then fails. Data grew, but the partition count stayed fixed. With two hundred partitions, twenty gigabytes is a hundred megabytes each. Two hundred gigabytes is one gigabyte each. Size partitions from data volume.

check.q: A job with a fixed partition count runs fine for months, then slows daily and fails. What is the most likely cause?
opts: Data grew, so each partition got larger until it spilled and then overflowed
check.why: The partition count stayed fixed while data grew, so every partition kept swelling. Compute partition count from data volume.

work: Search your code for collect and toPandas on large results and replace them with writes.
Derive shuffle partition counts from input size instead of hard-coding them.

title: Raising memory without adding executors

beats.say: A job fails at forty percent. How do you raise memory without adding executors?

show.text: Fails at 40%. More memory, same executors?

beats.say: You have three levers. Raise executor memory. Raise overhead if the container was killed. Or lower executor cores. Fewer tasks run at once in an executor, so each gets a bigger share. With eight gigabytes of execution memory, eight cores give about one gigabyte per task, four cores give two.

show.title: Execution memory per task (8 GB pool)

beats.say: Then say the key part: look for skew first. Extra memory on a skewed job only moves the failure to next month, when the hot key grows. And bigger executors cost more on every single run.

show.title: Memory hides *skew*, it does not fix it

nodes.label: More memory
nodes.sub: works for now, costs every run

check.q: What is the best answer to: how do you raise memory without adding executors?
opts: Raise memory or overhead, or lower cores per executor, but check for skew first
check.why: Fewer cores mean fewer concurrent tasks, so each task gets more memory. But skew is the root cause that extra memory only postpones.

work: Before resizing, compare the longest task to the median task in the failing stage to check for skew.
If memory must grow, try fewer cores per executor before bigger executors, and price both.
Alert on spill volume so you catch growth before the job fails.

title: The shuffle as a mail room

beats.say: Why does one step in a Spark job take longer than all the others put together?
Picture one hundred mail clerks. Each holds a mixed pile of letters for many cities. Every clerk sorts their pile into one bin per city and leaves the bins on a shelf.
Now each city has one courier. Every courier must visit every clerk and collect that city's bin. With fifty cities, that is five thousand pickups.
That is a shuffle. Sorting is quick. The slow part is the walking, which in Spark means disk writes and network transfer. So moving less data makes a faster job.

check.q: In the mail room picture, what makes the shuffle slow?
check.why: The sort is cheap. The many-to-many trips, which are disk and network transfer in Spark, dominate the cost.

work: Find the slowest stage in a Spark job and check whether it is a shuffle.
Ask of each join: how many bytes must move between machines?

title: How a shuffle moves data

beats.say: A join in Spark moves data between machines. How, exactly?
First, each map task sorts its output by target partition and writes it to its own local disk. One file per task, with an index of where each partition starts.
Then each reduce task fetches its slice from every map task over the network. A thousand map tasks and two hundred reducers means two hundred thousand fetches.

The setting spark dot sql dot shuffle dot partitions picks the reducer count. The default is two hundred. With one hundred gigabytes, that is five hundred megabytes each. Aim for one hundred to two hundred megabytes, so roughly eight hundred partitions.

check.q: A shuffle moves 100 GB and uses the default 200 partitions. What is the main concern?
opts: Partitions average 500 MB, risking spills or out of memory
Partitions average 5 MB, making tiny tasks
The shuffle will skip the disk
check.why: 100 GB divided by 200 is about 500 MB each, well above the 100 to 200 MB target, so tasks may spill or fail.

work: Divide each big shuffle's size by its partition count and compare to 100 to 200 MB.
Look at the Spark UI shuffle read and write sizes per stage.

title: Too few or too many partitions

beats.say: Why is two hundred shuffle partitions right only by accident?
Too few, and each partition is huge. Executor memory fills, data spills to disk, or the task dies with an out of memory error.
Too many, and you launch thousands of tiny tasks. Scheduling overhead dominates, and the write produces thousands of small files that slow every later read.
Adaptive execution now merges small shuffle partitions after seeing real sizes. That helps with too many, but still start with a sensible number, aiming for one hundred to two hundred megabytes each.

show.title: Rules of thumb
items: Do not rely on the default

check.q: Which symptom points to too few shuffle partitions?
opts: Tasks spilling to disk or running out of memory
check.why: Few partitions means each is large, so memory fills and tasks spill or fail. Tiny files point to too many.

work: Check spill metrics in the Spark UI for your heaviest stages.
Enable adaptive execution and still set a deliberate partition count for big jobs.

title: Repartition versus coalesce

beats.say: You need fewer output files. Do you reach for repartition or coalesce?
Repartition does a full shuffle. Every row moves, so partitions come out evenly sized. It can raise or lower the count, and it can hash on a new key.
Coalesce just glues neighbouring partitions together. There is no shuffle, so it is cheap. But it can only lower the count, and sizes may end up uneven.
Use coalesce to cut file count before a write. Use repartition when you need balance or a different key. Beware coalescing to a tiny number: it can squeeze earlier work into few tasks.

check.q: You want to raise partitions from 50 to 400 with even sizes. Which do you use?
check.why: Coalesce can only lower the count. Repartition shuffles and can both raise it and balance it.

work: Replace repartition with coalesce on pre-write file compaction when balance does not matter.
Check partition size spread after any coalesce.

title: Shrink the shuffle before it runs

beats.say: The cheapest shuffle is the one you never run. How do you shrink it?

Cost is disk, network and serialisation, multiplied by data volume. So cut volume first. Filter rows and select only needed columns before the join. If a table has forty columns and you need five, you move far fewer bytes.
Aggregate before joining where the logic allows. Summing two billion events down to ten million customer rows first means the join shuffles ten million, not two billion.
The catch: this only works when the maths allows it. Sums and counts combine safely. Exact distinct counts or medians do not, without extra care.

check.q: Which change most directly cuts shuffle cost?
opts: Filtering and selecting columns before the join
check.why: Shuffle cost scales with bytes moved, so dropping rows and columns before the join reduces everything downstream.

work: Review top joins for filters and column pruning that can move earlier.
Check whether a pre-aggregation is mathematically safe before adding it.

title: Broadcast and reuse partitioning

beats.say: What if the big table never had to move at all?
Broadcast the small table. Spark copies it to every executor, and each joins locally against its slice of the big side. No shuffle on the big table.
The trade-off is memory. The copy sits on every executor and passes through the driver, so a table that grows can cause out of memory failures. Use it for megabytes, not gigabytes.
Also reuse partitioning. If data is already partitioned by customer, a following group by or join on customer skips another shuffle. Change the key, and you pay again.

check.q: When is a broadcast join a risky choice?
opts: When the small table may grow to gigabytes
When the big table is large
When the join key is an integer
check.why: Broadcasting copies the table to every executor and through the driver, so growth can exhaust memory.

work: List joins that broadcast today and monitor the size of their small side.
Order consecutive operations to share one key and avoid repeated shuffles.

title: Spark as a kitchen brigade

beats.say: How do you cook ten thousand meals in an hour? Not with one faster chef.
Picture a big kitchen. A head chef reads the order, writes the plan, and splits it into small jobs for many cooks at their own stations.
Chopping happens at every station without talking. But when all the onions must go to one pot, cooks stop and carry them across the room. That carrying is slow.
That kitchen is Spark. The head chef is the driver, the cooks are executors, and carrying food between stations is a shuffle. Good plans carry as little as possible.

check.q: In this picture, what makes a big Spark job slow?
opts: The head chef reading the order
check.why: Moving data between machines, a shuffle, is the costly step; work done in place is cheap.

work: Look at one slow job and count how many times its data moves between machines.
Ask whether the data would fit on one machine before reaching for a cluster.

title: Driver, stages and tasks

beats.say: You write ten lines of Spark and nothing runs. Why?
Transformations only build a plan. When you call an action such as write or count, the driver optimizes the plan and cuts it into stages, at every point where data must be shuffled.
Inside a stage, filters and selects are chained, and one task runs per partition. Four hundred eighty partitions means four hundred eighty tasks, spread over the executor cores.
If a task fails, the driver retries it. If an executor dies and takes its shuffle files with it, the parent stage reruns. So: one action, stages between shuffles, a task per partition.

show.title: Remember
items: Task: one partition on one core

check.q: A stage reads 300 partitions with only narrow steps. How many tasks does it run?
check.why: A stage runs one task per partition; executors only decide how many run at the same time.

work: Open the Spark UI for a job and match each stage to an exchange in the plan.
Check task counts against partition counts for your widest stage.

title: Shuffles, broadcasts and AQE

beats.say: Why does a join on two big tables cost so much more than a filter?
A shuffle sends every row to the partition that owns its key. Map tasks write their output to local disk, reducers fetch it over the network, and the next stage waits for all of it.
A broadcast join skips it. The small table is copied to every executor as a lookup map, so the big table is read in place and never moves.

chip.text: No shuffle of the big side

beats.say: Adaptive query execution re-plans at each stage boundary using real sizes. It turns a join into a broadcast when one side proves small, and merges tiny partitions.

check.q: Why does a broadcast join avoid shuffling the large table?
opts: Every executor gets the small table, so large rows are joined where they are
check.why: With the small side copied everywhere, each large partition can be joined in place.

work: Find a sort-merge join in one of your plans and check whether one side is small after filters.
Confirm adaptive execution is on and look for coalesced partitions in the SQL tab.

title: Skew and salting

beats.say: Your job has nine hundred tasks. Eight hundred ninety nine finish in ten seconds. One takes thirty minutes. Why?
One key, say one big city, holds most of the rows. After the shuffle, all of them land in one partition, and one task must read them alone.

Try adaptive skew join first: it splits a partition bigger than five times the median. If that is not enough, salt. Add a random number, zero to nine, to the hot key, and copy the small side ten times, once per salt.
The cost is a small side ten times larger, so salt only the hot keys, and size the salt from what you measured.

show.title: Salting rules
items: Copy the other side per salt

check.q: After salting a hot key with ten values, why must the other side be copied ten times?
opts: So every salted row still finds its match
check.why: Each salted hot row carries one of ten salts, so the other side must exist with every salt for the join to match.

work: Sort a slow stage by task duration and compare the maximum to the median.
Count rows per join key and list the top ten before choosing a fix.

title: Memory, spill and out of memory

beats.say: Spilling to disk keeps a job alive. So why do jobs still die of out of memory?

After a small reserved slice, sixty percent of the executor heap is shared by execution, meaning joins, sorts and shuffles, and storage for cached data. Execution can push the cache out, but only down to a protected half.

When a sort runs out of room, Spark writes sorted runs to disk and merges them later. Slower, but safe. Out of memory comes from things that cannot spill: a giant skewed or exploded partition, an oversized broadcast, or collect on the driver.

chip.text: Huge rows and broadcasts cannot spill

beats.say: And Python workers live outside the heap, in memory overhead. Past that limit, Kubernetes or YARN kills the container.

check.q: A container is killed for memory while its Java heap is half empty. What is the likely cause?
opts: Python or off heap buffers exceeded memory overhead
check.why: Python workers and Arrow buffers use memoryOverhead outside the heap; exceeding it gets the container killed.

work: Read spill and garbage collection time for your largest stage.
Check memoryOverhead on any job that runs Python UDFs.

title: Catalyst and whole-stage codegen

beats.say: The same logic as a DataFrame often runs many times faster than a Python UDF. Where does the speed come from?

Catalyst is the optimizer. It checks names against the catalog, pushes filters down to the file scan, drops unused columns, then picks a physical plan, such as broadcast or sort merge, from size statistics.

Tungsten runs it. Rows sit in a compact binary form with little garbage collection, and whole-stage code generation fuses scan, filter and project into one tight generated loop, instead of one function call per row per operator.
A Python UDF is a black box to both. Filters cannot pass through it, and rows must leave the binary format. Prefer built in functions, or pandas UDFs over Arrow.

check.q: Why does a plain Python UDF slow a Spark query?
opts: Catalyst cannot see inside it and rows must be converted for Python
check.why: The UDF is opaque to the optimizer and breaks the binary row format and code generation.

work: Run explain on a slow query and look for operators without a star.
Replace one Python UDF with a built in function and compare run time.

title: Should we use Spark at all?

beats.say: A team wants Spark for a fifty gigabyte daily job. Is that the right call?
Under a few hundred gigabytes, DuckDB or Polars on one machine often finishes before a cluster even starts, at a fraction of the cost.

Spark earns its place on terabytes of joins and backfills over the lake, with SQL and Python side by side and open table formats. Flink wins for low latency stateful streams. The warehouse wins for plain SQL. Ray wins for GPU training.

chip.text: Match the engine to the job

beats.say: So ask three things first: how big, how fast, and who will own it.

check.q: A daily job reads 40 GB and needs results in an hour. What is often the cheaper choice?
opts: A single-node engine such as DuckDB or Polars
check.why: Data that fits on one machine is usually faster and cheaper without a cluster.

work: List your Spark jobs by input size and flag any under a hundred gigabytes.
For one streaming job, write down the latency it truly needs.

title: Owning, paying and leaving Spark

beats.say: Who gets paged when a Spark job runs out of memory at three in the morning?
A platform team owns the runtime, versions, cluster policies, and cost guardrails such as auto termination and spot instances. Pipeline teams own their jobs, their sizing and their skew.

chip.text: Tag cost per job and team

beats.say: It fails as stragglers from skew, out of memory, lost spot executors breaking shuffles, a driver choking on millions of small files, and a bill that grows faster than the data.
Move off when data shrinks to one machine, when work becomes low latency streaming, or when the warehouse runs the SQL cheaper.

check.q: Which belongs to the platform team rather than the pipeline team?
check.why: The platform owns the runtime and guardrails; pipeline teams own their jobs, sizing and data shape.

work: Check that every cluster has auto termination and a cost tag.
Write a one-page owner map for Spark: platform, pipelines, on-call.
